newsitem.title: USA: Diabetic women at higher risk for early menopause.
newsitem.headline: Diabetic women at higher risk for early menopause.

text.p: Women who developed diabetes early in life are at a greater risk for premature menopause and the consequent increased risks of heart disease, according to a report released on Saturday at the American Diabetes Association meeting here.
Researchers quickly called for further studies of their findings that for women with type 1 diabetes, menopause appears to start almost a decade earlier than for other women.

Nearly 16 million Americans suffer from diabetes and 8.8 million of them are women. However, the number that suffer from type 1 diabetes -- which usually begins in childhood or adolescence is much smaller -- some 700,000 Americans, according to the ADA.

The study, part of an ongoing review at the University of Pittsburgh Graduate School of Public Health, compared more than 100 sets of sisters - one of whom suffered from type 1 diabetes, while her sibling did not.
"Women with type 1 diabetes hit menopause on average at 40.7 years, compared to 49.9 for their non-diabetic sisters," according to researcher Janice Dornan.

Diabetics are two to four times more likely to have heart disease. Post-menopausal women are also at a higher risk for heart disease, so diabetic women who reach menopause prematurely also face an elevated risk of heart disease earlier.

"The take-home message of this study for women with diabetes is that they should be extra vigilant about adopting a heart healthy lifestyle, by not smoking, eating a low-fat diet, exercising regularly, trying to maintain ideal weight and keeping their diabetes in good control," Dorman said.

She added, "when menopause occurs, especially if it is premature, careful consideration should be given to hormone replacement therapy that has been shown to lower cardiovascular disease risks in women."
Another, much smaller study released at the three day scientific session found that women suffering from type 1 diabetes can also develop painless lumps in their breasts.

"Women with diabetes and their doctors need to know about this problem - and that it does not appear to increase breast cancer risk - to help ease anxiety when nodules arise," Mayo Clinic researcher Timothy O'Brien said.
Scientists for both studies called for further research to be done to confirm their findings.
